grand_strategy.reading:
Iran in October 2026 runs the strategy of a regime that has lost the war it
prepared for and cannot afford to concede it. Between June 2025 and February
2026 its three layers of security collapsed one after another: the nuclear
sites, the proxy belt (Assad gone in December 2024, Hezbollah gutted) and
finally the leadership itself, when the US-Israeli campaign killed Ali Khamenei
and then Larijani. What is left is a system run by the Revolutionary Guards
behind an unseen successor, with the economy at near-zero oil income, a
population it shot at in January, and one lever: the Strait of Hormuz and the
ability to hit Gulf infrastructure. Luttwak's logic shows in how that lever
works against its owner: each use of it hardens an adversary (the UAE,
Qatar, Saudi Arabia) that Tehran needs as a neighbour, and each hedge it
builds (enriched uranium, the NPT-exit bill) justifies the next strike. The
great powers it counted on (Russia, China) offer words, oil purchases and
mediation, not defence, and both want Hormuz open more than they want Iran
to win. Two signals that are not rows: Mojtaba Khamenei has not been seen in
public since his appointment, and the Majlis has not yet voted on leaving the
NPT: the one move Tehran has not made is the one that would end the ambiguity.
The cards that matter are Washington's (whether it still wants regime change,
as Netanyahu does, or a deal on enrichment, as Vance's 7 October language on a
'meaningful reduction' suggests) and Beijing's (whether it will trade its
oil dependence for pressure on Tehran).

The atlas reads it as a war between two states each of which would accept the other's defeat, with talks as an instrument of the war, not a thaw.
